blocks.text:
### How to use this guide

- **Who this is for.** A Java full stack developer who must explain, and diagnose, what the operating system does beneath a running service: process and thread management, memory, files, I/O, containers and synchronisation.
- **Every chapter follows the same steps:** (1) the concept and the problem it solves, (2) the mechanism, shown with diagrams, (3) a worked trace or calculation, (4) a hands-on experiment with real commands, C or Java code, (5) **real-world incidents**, each presented as symptoms, diagnosis, root cause, fix and prevention, and (6) the questions interviewers ask, with answers.
- **How to study.** Read each diagram before the prose and narrate it aloud. Reproduce every experiment on a Linux machine or virtual machine (never on a production host). Treat each incident as an exercise: cover the diagnosis, decide which command to run first, then compare with the text.
- **Running the code.** Save a Java listing as `Main.java` and run `java Main.java`; compile C with `gcc -O0 -o demo` `demo.c`. Terminal sessions begin with `$`. Output shown was produced on the build machine unless labelled typical.
- **Scope.** The focus is Linux, the platform on which most Java services run, together with the JVM and container behaviour that interacts with it. Windows and macOS are mentioned only where the difference matters.

A computer consists of processors, memory, storage devices and network adapters, each with its own programming interface and its own failure modes. A program that talked to this hardware directly would need to contain a disk driver, a memory allocator, a network stack and a scheduler, and two such programs running at the same time would overwrite each other's data. The operating system exists to remove both problems. It presents every program with a uniform, simplified machine, and it arbitrates between programs that compete for the real one.

For a Java developer the operating system is rarely visible in source code, yet it determines the behaviour of every deployed service. The size of the heap that the JVM selects, the number of threads that can be created, the point at which a request becomes slow, and the exit status that a container orchestrator reports are all decisions or side effects of the kernel. This chapter defines the operating system precisely, distinguishes the kernel from the rest of the system, and traces a single line of Java output through every layer between the source code and the hardware.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The three functions of an operating system

An operating system performs three functions that are easier to understand separately than as a single definition.

- **Resource management.** The processor, memory, storage and network bandwidth are finite. The kernel decides which thread runs on which core, which pages stay in memory, and which request is served next by a disk.
- **Abstraction.** Hardware details are hidden behind stable interfaces. A program opens a file, not a set of disk sectors; it uses a socket, not a network card queue; it addresses virtual memory, not physical frames.
- **Protection and isolation.** One program must not read or corrupt the memory of another, and an unprivileged program must not issue instructions that control the hardware. The processor enforces the rule, and the kernel configures the processor to do so.

blocks.text:
#### Kernel and user space

The **kernel** is the part of the operating system that runs with full hardware privileges and is always resident in memory. Everything else runs in **user space**: shells, compilers, the JVM, web servers, and also the system utilities that are conventionally considered part of the operating system, such as `ps`, `systemd` and the C library. A *distribution* such as Ubuntu is the Linux kernel plus a large collection of user-space programs. Linux itself names only the kernel.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.text: Kernel: the privileged component of an operating system that manages the processor, memory and devices, and that user programs enter only through a controlled interface, the system call.

The separation is enforced by the processor. x86-64 processors define four privilege levels, called rings. Linux and Windows use two of them: ring 0 for the kernel and ring 3 for applications. The current ring is recorded in the low two bits of the code segment register. Privileged instructions, such as those that load page tables, disable interrupts or halt the processor, are legal only in ring 0. A program in ring 3 can leave the ring only through designated entry points, which are the system call instruction, interrupts and processor faults.

blocks.text: The separation can be demonstrated directly. The program in the following listing executes `HLT`, an instruction that stops the processor until the next interrupt, from user mode.

blocks.title: priv.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -o priv priv.c && ./priv; echo "exit status $?"
about to execute HLT in user mode
/bin/bash: line 23:  2561 Segmentation fault      ./priv
exit status 139
$ strace -e trace=none ./priv 2>&1 | tail -2
--- SIGSEGV {si_signo=SIGSEGV, si_code=SI_KERNEL, si_addr=NULL} ---
+++ killed by SIGSEGV +++
blocks.title: Privileged instruction in user mode (Linux 6.18.44, x86-64)

blocks.text:
The processor raised a general protection fault. The kernel's fault handler found that the faulting code belonged to a user process and converted the fault into the signal `SIGSEGV`. The marker `SI_KERNEL` in the signal information states that the kernel itself generated the signal, not a bad memory reference by the program. The shell reports the exit status 139, which is 128 plus the signal number 11. The same arithmetic recurs for container exit codes later in this chapter.

#### Kernel architectures

Operating-system designs differ in how much functionality runs in ring 0. The choice is a trade between speed, robustness and the amount of privileged code that must be trusted.

Linux is monolithic but not static. Drivers and file systems can be built as **loadable kernel modules**, which are linked into the running kernel on demand; the modularity is organisational, because a loaded module runs in ring 0 with full privilege.

#### Where a Java program sits

A Java program never invokes the kernel directly. Every request passes through the layers shown below. The JVM translates bytecode into native code and implements Java library methods with native methods. Those native methods call functions in the C library, and the C library contains the thin wrappers that execute the system call instruction.

**Java code** System.out.println("Hello, JVM"); **Observed with strace -f**

blocks.code:
798 clone3(...) = 799
799 write(1, "Hello, JVM\n", 11)

blocks.text: **JVM (libjvm.so, thread tid 799 "main")**
PrintStream \> FileOutputStream.writeBytes (JNI)

blocks.code:
1457 syscalls in the whole run
18 threads (tids) seen

blocks.text:
**C library (libc.so.6)** write(): rax=1, rdi=1, rsi=buf, rdx=11, SYSCALL

**user space (ring 3) above**

**kernel space (ring 0) below** **Kernel** syscall entry \> VFS \> file or tty driver \> block / char device **Cost of the boundary**

function call:    1 ns
getppid() trap:  ~120 ns

blocks.text:
**Hardware** `same call under strace:` CPU, RAM, disk controller, NIC, UART `~13000 ns`

*Figure 1.4. The call* `System.out.println` *reaches the kernel as one* `write` *system call; the numbers in the side panels were* *measured on the build machine and appear again in the worked trace and in the system call chapter.*

Two consequences follow. First, any operation that touches a device, the clock, the network or the memory map has a cost that includes a ring transition. Second, every observable behaviour of a JVM is ultimately a sequence of system calls, which makes tools that observe system calls, principally `strace`, applicable to Java programs without changes to the code.

### Worked trace

The following steps trace `System.out.println("Hello, JVM")` from a terminal. The values come from `strace -f` runs of the program `Hello` on the build machine (Linux 6.18.44, OpenJDK 21.0.12); thread identifiers vary between runs.

1. The shell calls `fork` and then `execve("/usr/bin/java", ...)`. The kernel replaces the address space of the child with that of the `java` launcher. The launcher has thread identifier 798 in this run.
2. The launcher loads `libjvm.so` with `openat` and `mmap`, then calls `clone3` with the flags `CLONE_VM|CLONE_FS|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_SIGHAND|CLONE_THREAD`. The new native thread, identifier 799, becomes the Java `main` thread. Linux treats it as a task that shares the address space of its creator.
3. The JVM maps `lib/modules` (the class library image, about 140 MB) and the class data sharing archive `classes.jsa`, then starts the garbage collector, compiler and housekeeping threads. Eighteen thread identifiers appear in the full trace.
4. The bytecode of `main` calls `PrintStream.println`. The text is encoded to bytes and handed to `FileOutputStream.writeBytes`, a native method.
5. The native method calls the C library function `write(1, buf, 11)`. The wrapper places 1 in `rax` (the number of `write` in the x86-64 system call table), the descriptor 1 in `rdi`, the buffer address in `rsi` and the length 11 in `rdx`, and executes `SYSCALL`.
6. The processor switches to ring 0, loads the kernel stack and jumps to the system call entry code. The kernel indexes its system call table with `rax`, runs `ksys_write`, which resolves descriptor 1 to the terminal or pipe through the virtual file system, and copies 11 bytes into it.
7. The kernel places the return value 11 in `rax` and executes `SYSRET`. The processor returns to ring 3. The wrapper returns 11 to the JVM, which returns normally to the Java code.

The trace line for step 5 is:

blocks.code:
$ strace -f -o java.full java Hello > /dev/null
$ grep 'write(1' java.full
799   write(1, "Hello, JVM\n", 11 <unfinished ...>
$ wc -l java.full
1821 java.full
blocks.title: The single system call behind println

blocks.text:
The `<unfinished ...>` marker is an artefact of `strace -f`: another thread produced output between the entry and the exit of the call, so `strace` prints the entry and the result on separate lines.

$ java -version 2>&1 | head -1
openjdk version "21.0.12.1" 2026-08-18
blocks.title: Kernel, distribution and process 1 on the build machine

blocks.text:
The kernel version is independent of the distribution release. The first process on this machine is not `systemd`; the machine is a micro virtual machine whose kernel starts a purpose-built init program directly. The boot chapter explains the difference. On a typical server or in a full virtual machine, `ps -p 1` reports `systemd`, and inside a container it reports the container's entry point.

#### Observe the native threads of a JVM

The JVM maps each Java platform thread to one kernel thread, and the kernel exposes every thread as an entry in `/proc/PID/task`. The program `Sleeper` prints its process identifier and sleeps; it was started with `-Xmx64m -Xss512k`.

blocks.code:
$ java -Xmx64m -Xss512k Sleeper 60000 &
pid=8323
$ ls /proc/8323/task | wc -l
18
$ for t in $(ls /proc/8323/task); do echo "$t $(cat /proc/8323/task/$t/comm)"; done | head -8
8323 java
8325 java
8326 GC Thread#0
8327 G1 Main Marker
8328 G1 Conc#0
8329 G1 Refine#0
8330 G1 Service
8331 VM Periodic Tas
$ grep -E 'State|Threads|VmSize|VmRSS' /proc/8323/status
State:  S (sleeping)
VmSize:  2646632 kB
VmRSS:     40740 kB
Threads:        18
blocks.title: Threads of an idle JVM (typical output; identifiers vary)

blocks.text:
An idle JVM that executes `Thread.sleep` owns eighteen kernel threads, 2.6 GB of virtual address space and 40 MB of resident memory. The thread named `java` with the lowest identifier is the launcher thread; the second is the Java `main` thread. The comm field is limited to 15 characters, which explains the truncated names. The large gap between virtual size and resident size is a first example of the difference between address space reserved by the JVM and memory that the kernel has actually backed with physical pages. The memory part of this book treats it fully.

#### Compare the cost of starting a native and a managed program

blocks.code:
$ time ./hello > /dev/null
real    0m0.002s
user    0m0.001s
sys     0m0.000s
$ time java Hello > /dev/null
real    0m0.046s
user    0m0.039s
sys     0m0.013s
blocks.title: Elapsed time of a C hello and a Java hello (measured, typical)

blocks.text:
The native program issues 34 system calls; the JVM issues about 1450, creates 17 additional threads and maps hundreds of megabytes of address space. Most of the 46 ms is the work of preparing the runtime, which is the reason that short-lived command-line tools are rarely written in Java and that serverless platforms care about JVM start-up.

### Real-world incidents

#### Incident: Spring Boot service cannot bind port 80 after migration to a non-root user

**Scenario.** A team hardens a Spring Boot service by running it under an unprivileged account instead of root. The service previously listened on port 80 behind a load balancer health check. The new release starts on the staging host, which runs as root during tests, and fails on the production host.

**Symptoms.** The unit enters a restart loop. The application log contains `java.net.BindException: Permission` `denied` shortly after the banner, and the load balancer marks every instance unhealthy.

**Diagnosis.** The exception text is the message of the system call error `EACCES`. The first step is to confirm which call failed and what the kernel policy is. The reproduction uses a minimal server socket program.

blocks.title: Bind.java

blocks.code:
$ id -u
0
$ java Bind 80
listening on 80
$ setpriv --reuid=65534 --regid=65534 --clear-groups java Bind 80
Exception in thread "main" java.net.BindException: Permission denied
        at java.base/sun.nio.ch.Net.bind0(Native Method)
        at java.base/sun.nio.ch.Net.bind(Net.java:577)
        ...
$ setpriv --reuid=65534 --regid=65534 --clear-groups \
    strace -f -e trace=bind java Bind 80 2>&1 | grep 'bind('
5260  bind(4, {sa_family=AF_INET, sin_port=htons(80), ...}, 16) = -1 EACCES (Permission denied)
$ cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_unprivileged_port_start
1024
blocks.title: Reproduction as uid 65534 (the nobody account)

blocks.text:
The `strace` line shows the failing system call, `bind`, with the result `EACCES`. The sysctl `net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start` is the policy: ports below 1024 may be bound only by a process that holds the capability `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` in its effective set. The root user passes the check because root holds all capabilities, which is also why the staging tests succeeded.

**Fixes (each changes one input)** new ServerSocket(80) **bind succeeds** JVM calls bind(fd, 0.0.0.0:80)

1. listen on 8080;

proxy or load balancer maps 80

*changes the port* port \< ip\_unprivileged\_port\_start no (1024)?

1. AmbientCapabilities=

CAP\_NET\_BIND\_SERVICE

yes *changes the capability set*

process has yes CAP\_NET\_BIND\_SERVICE? 3. sysctl ip\_unprivileged\_port\_start (host-wide, least preferred)

no *changes the policy*

**EACCES \> BindException:** **Permission denied**

*Figure 1.5. The kernel decides the outcome of* `bind` *from two facts, the port number and the capability set of the caller; each fix* *changes one of those facts.*

**Root cause.** The service was moved to an unprivileged account without granting it the right to use a privileged port. The failure is deterministic and independent of the Java code.

**Fix.** The immediate mitigation is to move the application to a port above 1023, for example 8080, and to let the load balancer or a reverse proxy listen on port 80. The permanent options, in order of preference, are:

1. Bind to port 8080 and map the port externally (container port mapping, load balancer listener, or an `iptables` redirect). No privilege is involved.
2. Grant only the needed capability to the process. With systemd this is `AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`. The following run shows the effect with `setpriv`:

blocks.code:
$ setpriv --reuid=65534 --regid=65534 --clear-groups \
    --inh-caps +net_bind_service --ambient-caps +net_bind_service java Bind 80
listening on 80
blocks.title: The same unprivileged user with one capability

blocks.text:
1. Lower the sysctl `net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start` for the whole host. This weakens a host-wide boundary for one service and is the least preferred option.

**Prevention.** Run the production start-up path under the production account in a pre-production environment. A start-up test that executes the unit as the service user would have caught the failure before release. Document the listening port in the deployment descriptor, and prefer ports above 1023 for application processes.

#### Incident: the orchestrator reports exit code 143 for a service that stopped cleanly

**Scenario.** A deployment pipeline stops a Java service by sending `SIGTERM` and treats any non-zero exit status as a failed stop. After a harmless redeployment, the pipeline marks every stop as failed and rolls the release back.

**Symptoms.** The service log ends with the normal shutdown messages, but the supervisor records `exited, code=143` or `Terminated`. Container dashboards show exit code 143 with no error in the log. **Diagnosis.** A shell and most supervisors encode death by signal as 128 plus the signal number. The statuses can be reproduced without any application bug. The program `Hook` registers a shutdown hook and sleeps.

blocks.title: Hook.java

blocks.code:
$ java Sleeper 60000 > s2.out & P=$!; sleep 2; kill -TERM $P; wait $P; echo "TERM: $?"
TERM: 143
$ java Sleeper 60000 > s3.out & P=$!; sleep 2; kill -KILL $P; wait $P; echo "KILL: $?"
KILL: 137
$ java Hook > h.out & P=$!; sleep 2; kill -TERM $P; wait $P; echo "exit=$?"; cat h.out
exit=143
started
shutdown hook ran
blocks.title: Exit status after SIGTERM and SIGKILL

blocks.text: The last run uses a program that registers a shutdown hook. The hook ran, so the stop was orderly, and the status was still 143. The JVM handles `SIGTERM` by running the shutdown hooks and then terminating, and the termination is reported as death by signal 15.

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The pipeline interpreted any non-zero status as failure. The status 143 is the expected status of a JVM that received `SIGTERM`, whether or not the shutdown was clean.

**Fix.** Configure the supervisor to accept the status: `SuccessExitStatus=143` in a systemd unit, or compare the exit code with 143 in the pipeline. The actual health of the shutdown is better judged from the log (the shutdown hooks completed) and from the absence of status 137.

**Prevention.** Treat 143 as success and 137 as an alert condition. A 137 after a stop request means that the process ignored or outlived `SIGTERM` and was killed by `SIGKILL` after the grace period (`TimeoutStopSec` in systemd, `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` in Kubernetes); in a container without a memory limit increase it can also be the kernel out-of-memory killer, which the memory part distinguishes by reading the kernel log.

### Questions to expect

#### Questions and model answers

1. **What is the difference between the kernel and the operating system?** The kernel is the privileged core that manages the processor, memory and devices. The operating system, in the common sense, also includes the system libraries, the init system and the utilities that make the kernel usable. Linux is a kernel; Ubuntu is an operating system built around it.
2. **Why do user programs call the kernel through system calls instead of jumping into it?** The processor allows ring 3 code to enter ring 0 only at addresses that the kernel registered. This prevents arbitrary code from running with kernel privilege and lets the kernel validate every argument.
3. **Name the privilege levels used by Linux on x86-64.** Ring 0 for the kernel and ring 3 for user programs. Rings 1 and 2 exist in the architecture but are not used.
4. **Compare monolithic and microkernel designs.** A monolithic kernel runs file systems, drivers and the network stack in one privileged address space: calls are fast and a driver fault can crash the system. A microkernel keeps only scheduling, IPC and address-space management in ring 0 and runs the rest as servers: faults are contained and each service call costs messages and context switches.
5. **Is Linux a microkernel because it has loadable modules?** No. Modules are loaded into ring 0 and share the kernel address space; they provide modularity of packaging, not isolation.
6. **How does a Java** `println` **reach the screen?** Bytecode calls `PrintStream`, which calls a native method; the native method calls libc `write`, which executes `SYSCALL`; the kernel resolves the file descriptor through the virtual file system to a terminal or pipe and copies the bytes.
7. **A Java thread corresponds to what in Linux?** One kernel task created by `clone`, listed under `/proc/PID/task`, scheduled independently. Virtual threads in Java 21 are different: they are scheduled by the JVM onto a small number of platform threads.
8. **What does exit status 139 mean?** The process was killed by signal 11 (`SIGSEGV`), because 139 is 128 plus 11. Status 143 is `SIGTERM` and status 137 is `SIGKILL`.
9. **Why can a non-root service not listen on port 80, and how is it permitted safely?** Binding below 1024 requires `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`. The service is granted that capability only, or it listens on a high port behind a proxy or load balancer.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
The operating system multiplexes, protects and abstracts the hardware; the kernel is its privileged part and runs in ring 0, while every other program, including the JVM, runs in ring 3.

- Linux is a monolithic kernel with loadable modules; a distribution adds the user-space system.
- A Java program reaches the kernel through native methods, libc wrappers and the `SYSCALL` instruction; each Java platform thread is a kernel task visible in `/proc/PID/task`.
- Privileged instructions in user mode cause a fault that the kernel turns into `SIGSEGV`.
- Exit statuses above 128 encode death by signal: 137 is `SIGKILL`, 139 is `SIGSEGV`, 143 is `SIGTERM`.
- Policy failures such as `EACCES` on `bind` come from kernel checks on capabilities, not from the Java code.

An operating system is a program written for a particular machine, and several of its central mechanisms exist only because of properties of that machine: processors are far faster than memory, devices are far slower than processors, and several processors share one memory. This chapter reviews the hardware concepts needed to understand scheduling, virtual memory, interrupts and synchronisation, and it measures the memory hierarchy on the build machine, because the numbers explain behaviour that otherwise appears arbitrary.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Processor state and modes

The state of a running thread is small: the general-purpose registers, the instruction pointer (`RIP`), the stack pointer (`RSP`), the flags register and the segment and control registers. Switching from one thread to another means saving this state of the old thread in kernel memory and loading the state of the new one. That operation is a **context switch**, and its cost, together with the cost of the cache and TLB contents that become useless, is why thread counts matter.

Besides the privilege level, the processor has a mode that selects how addresses are interpreted. In 64-bit mode on the build machine (an Intel Xeon reporting 52 physical and 57 virtual address bits) the processor translates every address used by a program through page tables that the kernel maintains. The translation hardware is the memory management unit (MMU). It is what makes the isolation promised in the previous chapter enforceable, and the memory part of this book covers it in detail.

#### The memory hierarchy

A processor executes several instructions per nanosecond but main memory needs about a hundred nanoseconds to answer a request. Caches bridge the gap. Each level is smaller and faster than the one below it, and data moves between levels in fixed-size blocks called **cache lines**, 64 bytes on this machine.

blocks.text:
*L2 cache, and the final plateau is main memory. The 260 MiB L3 reported by* `lscpu` *is not usable by one tenant, because the hardware* *is shared.*

The practical law that follows is **locality**. Temporal locality means that recently used data is likely to be used again; spatial locality means that data near recently used data is likely to be used next. Programs and data structures that respect locality run several times faster than equivalent ones that do not, with identical instruction counts.

#### Interrupts, exceptions and the timer

Devices complete work at times that the processor cannot predict. Instead of polling, the processor lets a device raise an **interrupt**: an electrical or message signal that makes the processor stop the current instruction stream after the current instruction, save a small amount of state, switch to ring 0 and run a handler found through the interrupt descriptor table. Three kinds of event use this mechanism.

- **Hardware interrupts** come from devices (a network card with a received packet, a disk with a completed request) and from the timer.
- **Exceptions** are raised by the executing instruction itself: a page fault, a division by zero, an illegal instruction. The `HLT` experiment of the previous chapter was an exception.
- **Software interrupts and system calls** are deliberate entries into the kernel by the program.

blocks.text: The kernel splits interrupt work in two. The **top half** runs with interrupts masked and does the minimum, for example acknowledging the device and queueing the data. The **bottom half**, called a softirq or a tasklet, runs shortly afterwards with interrupts enabled and does the bulk of the work, for example protocol processing. Both are visible in `/proc`.

blocks.text:
The listing shows virtual devices (`virtio`) of a micro virtual machine; on bare metal the right-hand column names real network cards and disk controllers (`nvme0q1`, `eth0-TxRx-0`). The counters per CPU reveal whether interrupt load is spread: one CPU with a counter far above the others is a common cause of an uneven load. The `ctxt` line of `/proc/stat` counts all context switches since boot, and `intr` counts all interrupts.

The **timer interrupt** gives the kernel the periodic control that user programs cannot take away. On the build machine the kernel is configured with `CONFIG_HZ=250` (a periodic tick every 4 ms), and modern kernels additionally use high-resolution timers programmed for exact deadlines (`HRTIMER` row). At each tick the scheduler can decide that the running thread has used its time and must yield. Without a timer interrupt, a thread that never calls the kernel would hold the processor indefinitely.

#### Direct memory access

Copying a megabyte from a disk controller into memory one word at a time would occupy the processor for the entire duration of the transfer. **Direct memory access** (DMA) lets the controller write to memory by itself. The kernel programs the transfer, the processor runs other threads, and the device raises an interrupt when the transfer is complete.

blocks.text:
The consequence for application design is that an I/O wait is cheap for the processor, expensive for latency, and visible as the state of the waiting thread (state `S` or `D` in `ps`) and as the `wa` figure in `top` and `vmstat`.

#### Multicore processors and cache coherence

Each core has private L1 and L2 caches and shares an L3 cache and main memory with the other cores. When two cores cache the same line and one of them writes, the other copy becomes stale. Hardware **cache coherence** **protocols**, of which MESI is the textbook form, prevent this by tracking the state of every line and invalidating other copies before a write completes.

blocks.text: Coherence makes a shared-memory program correct at the hardware level, but not necessarily at the language level. Compilers and processors reorder independent operations, and a store may sit in a core's store buffer before other cores see it. The Java Memory Model and the `volatile` and `synchronized` constructs exist to restore ordering where it matters; the concurrency part of this book explains how they map to memory barriers. A related performance hazard is **false sharing**: two threads that write different variables placed on the same 64-byte line cause the line to bounce between their cores even though no data is shared logically. The standard remedy is padding or, in the JDK, the internal `@Contended` annotation.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: False sharing is real but difficult to measure on a shared virtual machine. Repeated trials of a two-thread counter on the build machine, with the counters adjacent or 128 bytes apart, gave overlapping timings (between 630 and 1210 ms per run), so the effect is not claimed here as a measurement. On dedicated hardware with pinned cores the difference is typically clear.

### Worked trace

#### A load that misses every cache level

The following sequence traces a read of a variable whose address is not in any cache, on the machine described above. The timings are the measured latencies of the table.

1. The thread executes `mov rax, [rbx]`. The MMU translates the virtual address in `rbx` to a physical address (the translation itself may need page-table reads, which are cached in the TLB; the memory part of this book follows it).
2. The core looks up the physical address in L1d, a 48 KiB cache of 64-byte lines. The lookup misses (about 2 ns have passed since the previous level began).
3. The L2 lookup misses, which adds about 5 ns of latency.
4. The L3 lookup misses. The request leaves the core through the shared interconnect.
5. The memory controller reads the 64-byte line from DRAM. Total latency is between 80 ns (16 MiB working set) and 176 ns (128 MiB working set) in the measurements.
6. The line is installed in L3, L2 and L1d, and `rax` is loaded. The following 7 loads from the same line (8 bytes each) hit in L1d and cost about 2 ns in total.

At a clock of 2.1 GHz, 100 ns correspond to 210 clock cycles, in which the core could have executed several hundred instructions. The prefetcher hides most of that for sequential access and none of it for random access, which is why the random-pointer experiment is slow and a sequential scan of the same memory is fast.

### Hands-on

#### Inspect the machine

blocks.code:
$ lscpu | grep -E 'Model name|^CPU\(s\)|Thread|Core|L1d|L2|L3|Hypervisor'
CPU(s):                                  2
Model name:                              Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor @ 2.10GHz
Thread(s) per core:                      1
Core(s) per socket:                      2
Hypervisor vendor:                       KVM
L1d cache:                               96 KiB (2 instances)
L2 cache:                                4 MiB (2 instances)
L3 cache:                                260 MiB (1 instance)
$ for i in 0 1 2 3; do d=/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache/index$i; \
    echo $(cat $d/level) $(cat $d/type) $(cat $d/size) line=$(cat $d/coherency_line_size); done
1 Data 48K line=64

2 Unified 2048K line=64
3 Unified 266240K line=64
blocks.title: Processor and cache facts (excerpt of lscpu and sysfs)

blocks.text:
The `Hypervisor vendor` line confirms that this machine is itself a guest, and that the figures for caches describe the host's hardware. On a cloud instance the same applies, which is one reason why measurements on shared virtual machines vary from run to run.

#### Measure the effect of access order

The next program sums a 4096 by 4096 matrix of `int` twice, once row by row and once column by column. Both versions perform 16,777,216 additions.

blocks.title: CacheDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java -Xmx300m CacheDemo.java
row-major   17 ms, column-major  211 ms (sum 16777216, 16777216)
row-major   12 ms, column-major  192 ms (sum 16777216, 16777216)
row-major    5 ms, column-major  180 ms (sum 16777216, 16777216)
blocks.title: Result (typical output; Java 21, 2 vCPUs, -Xmx300m)

blocks.text:
Row-major order reads consecutive addresses, so each 64-byte cache line serves 16 consecutive `int` values and the prefetcher keeps ahead of the loop. Column-major order touches a different row, and therefore a different cache line, on every access, and the 64 MiB matrix is far larger than the caches; each access pays a miss. The result is identical, the instruction count is nearly identical, and the second version is between 10 and 36 times slower.

#### Observe interrupts and context switches while a workload runs

blocks.code:
$ grep -E '^ctxt' /proc/stat; sleep 1; grep -E '^ctxt' /proc/stat
ctxt 30766906
ctxt 30769624
blocks.title: Context switches in one second (typical; the machine is shared with other workloads)

blocks.text:
The difference, 2,718 switches in one second on a machine with two cores, is the background activity of the system: every wake-up of a thread, every blocked call and every preemption is one switch. The figure becomes meaningful in comparison with a baseline, which the diagnostic chapters build with `vmstat` (column `cs`).

### Real-world incidents

**Incident: a nightly batch job becomes ten times slower after a refactoring that changed only the**

#### loop order

**Scenario.** A reporting job aggregates a large two-dimensional array of measurements held as `double[sensors][timestamps]`. A refactoring renames the loop variables and, in the process, swaps the nesting so that the inner loop iterates over sensors. The unit tests, which use ten by ten arrays, pass. The job runs on a Kubernetes node with a four-core limit.

**Symptoms.** The batch window grows from 25 minutes to more than three hours. CPU utilisation stays at 100 percent of one core, the heap is unchanged, garbage collection is quiet, and no error appears in any log. Profilers attribute the time to the innermost loop.

**Diagnosis.** CPU time without waiting, no GC, and a hot loop point to the memory system. The commands, in order, were:

1. `top -H -p PID` shows one thread at 100 percent in state `R` and `us` (user time) near 100 percent, so the process is computing, not waiting for I/O or the kernel.
2. `jcmd PID Thread.print` and a few repeated samples show the thread inside the aggregation method every time.
3. A micro-benchmark of the loop in isolation reproduces the slowdown with the sizes of production data (see the listing earlier in this chapter: 5 ms against 180 ms for the same additions).
4. `git diff` of the method shows the swapped loop order; no algorithmic change exists.

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The new loop order accessed memory with a stride of one row (32 KiB for 4096 doubles) so that every access missed the L1 and L2 caches and, for a working set above the cache sizes, paid the latency of main memory. The instruction count did not change; the number of cache misses grew by roughly the ratio of the cache line size to the element size: 8 for doubles and 16 for the 4-byte integers of the experiment.

**Fix.** Restore the row-major order, or iterate in blocks (tiling) when both orders are needed. Add a benchmark with realistic dimensions to the build.

**Prevention.** Small unit-test inputs cannot detect locality regressions, because they fit in the cache. A performance regression test with production-sized data, executed in continuous integration with a time budget, would have failed. Hardware counters (`perf stat` on a host where it is available, reporting cache misses and instructions per cycle) identify the cause directly; they are not available in the build environment of this book, so the evidence above is the measured timing.

**Incident: a latency-sensitive service slows down after switching from an array of primitives to a list**

#### of boxed values

**Scenario.** A price-aggregation service holds four million integer prices. A developer replaces an `int[]` with an `ArrayList<Integer>` to use the stream API conveniently. Entries arrive in random order and are inserted at random positions.

**Symptoms.** Throughput of the aggregation falls, the young-generation garbage collections become more frequent, and the 99th-percentile latency rises, although the total heap use grows by only a modest amount.

**Diagnosis.** The traversal of the collection is measured in isolation on the same hardware.

*Figure 1.12. An* `int[]` *stores values side by side; an* `ArrayList<Integer>` *stores references to separate objects, and when list* *order differs from allocation order each step of the loop is a dependent load that may miss every cache level.*

**Root cause.** Each element became a 4-byte reference (with compressed object pointers) to a separate 16-byte `Integer` object. Sequential allocation kept the objects near each other at first, so the in-order list stayed reasonably fast. After random insertion, consecutive list positions referred to objects scattered across the heap, so every element cost a dependent cache miss, the same pattern as the pointer-chasing experiment. The additional objects also increased allocation and young-collection work.

**Fix.** Use a primitive array or a primitive-specialised structure on hot paths, and keep boxed collections for the cold ones. Where the stream API is required, `IntStream` over an `int[]` retains the layout.

**Prevention.** Review the memory layout of data structures that are traversed in tight loops, and measure with representative sizes and order. The mean latency hides the problem; the percentile does not.

### Questions to expect

#### Questions and model answers

1. **What is a context switch and why is it costly?** Saving the registers of one thread and loading those of another, usually with a change of address space. The direct cost is small, a few microseconds at most; the larger cost is the loss of warm caches and TLB entries for the thread that was switched out.
2. **What is the difference between an interrupt and an exception?** An interrupt is asynchronous and comes from a device or timer; an exception is synchronous and caused by the executing instruction, such as a page fault or a division by zero. Both enter the kernel through the interrupt descriptor table.
3. **Why does the timer interrupt matter to the operating system?** It guarantees that the kernel regains control at regular intervals, which makes preemptive scheduling and timeouts possible even when a program never calls the kernel.
4. **What does DMA do and why does it improve utilisation?** DMA lets a device transfer data to or from memory without processor involvement. The processor programs the transfer, runs other work and receives an interrupt when the transfer is complete.
5. **Explain spatial and temporal locality with an example.** Spatial: reading `a[i+1]` right after `a[i]` uses data in the same cache line. Temporal: a loop counter reused in each iteration stays in a register or in L1. Row-major traversal of a Java matrix has both; column-major traversal loses the spatial part.
6. **What are the approximate access times of L1, L2, L3 and main memory?** On the measured machine, 2 ns, 5 to 6 ns, about 40 ns and 80 to 176 ns, which means a factor of 50 to 100 between L1 and main memory.
7. **What is cache coherence?** The guarantee that all cores observe a consistent value for a memory location in spite of private caches, implemented by protocols such as MESI that invalidate or update other copies when a core writes.
8. **What is false sharing?** Two threads writing different variables that lie on the same cache line cause the line to bounce between cores, which reduces throughput without any logical sharing. Padding or separate allocation avoids it.
9. **Why does the same loop run at different speeds in different orders although it executes the same** **instructions?** The speed is determined by cache misses, not by instruction count. A stride-one access pattern uses whole cache lines and is prefetched; a large stride does not.
10. **Why can a virtual machine report a 260 MiB L3 cache?** The guest reports the cache of the host processor, which is shared by many guests. The share available to one guest is smaller and varies with the load of the others.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Memory is two orders of magnitude slower than the processor cache, devices are slower still, and the operating system is built around hiding both gaps.

- The cache hierarchy on the build machine: about 2 ns (L1), 5 ns (L2), 40 ns (L3) and 80 to 176 ns (DRAM); locality decides which of these a program pays.
- Interrupts, exceptions and the timer return control to the kernel; DMA moves data without the processor, so blocking I/O does not waste a core.
- A context switch saves and restores register state; its hidden cost is the loss of warm caches.
- Cache coherence keeps cores consistent; false sharing and contended writes show up as lost throughput, not as wrong results.
- Data layout (primitive arrays against boxed lists, row against column order) can change run time by an order of magnitude with identical instruction counts.

A program cannot read a file, allocate memory from the kernel, create a thread or send a network packet by itself, because every one of those actions touches state that only ring 0 may modify. The **system call** is the interface through which user programs request such actions. It is the narrowest and most observable boundary in a running system: everything that a process does to the outside world, including everything that a JVM does, passes through it. A developer who can read a system call trace can answer questions that logs and profilers cannot, for example which file a service tried to open, which call it is blocked in, and how many times per second it enters the kernel.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The x86-64 Linux calling convention

A system call is a function call with a different calling convention and a privilege transition. On x86-64 Linux the convention is fixed by the kernel's application binary interface.

- The system call number is placed in `rax`.
- Up to six arguments are placed in `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `r10`, `r8` and `r9`, in that order. (The ordinary C calling convention uses `rcx` instead of `r10`; the `SYSCALL` instruction overwrites `rcx` with the return address.)
- The `SYSCALL` instruction switches the processor to ring 0, saves the return address in `rcx` and the flags in `r11`, and jumps to the address stored in a model-specific register, `LSTAR`, that the kernel set at boot.
- The kernel stores the result in `rax`. A value between -4095 and -1 is the negated error number (`errno`); any other value is a successful result.
- The `SYSRET` instruction returns to ring 3.

The kernel keeps a **system call table**, an array of function pointers indexed by the call number. On this build machine the header `asm/unistd_64.h` defines 373 numbers.

#### The C library wrapper and errno

Programs rarely execute `SYSCALL` themselves. The C library provides one wrapper per call that loads the registers, executes the instruction and converts a negative result into `errno` and a return value of -1. The disassembly of `write` in the C library of the build machine shows this directly.

blocks.code:
$ gdb -batch -ex 'disassemble write' /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 | head -12
Dump of assembler code for function __GI___libc_write:
   0x000000000011c830 <+0>:     endbr64
   0x000000000011c834 <+4>:     cmpb   $0x0,0xef805(%rip)        # 0x20c040 <__libc_single_threaded>
   0x000000000011c83b <+11>:    je     0x11c850 <__GI___libc_write+32>
   0x000000000011c83d <+13>:    mov    $0x1,%eax
   0x000000000011c842 <+18>:    syscall
   0x000000000011c844 <+20>:    cmp    $0xfffffffffffff000,%rax
   0x000000000011c84a <+26>:    ja     0x11c8a0 <__GI___libc_write+112>
   0x000000000011c84c <+28>:    ret
   0x000000000011c8a0 <+112>:   mov    0xe7551(%rip),%rdx        # 0x203df8
   0x000000000011c8a7 <+119>:   neg    %eax
   0x000000000011c8a9 <+121>:   mov    %eax,%fs:(%rdx)
blocks.title: The write wrapper in libc.so.6 (Ubuntu glibc, trimmed)

blocks.text:
The instruction at offset +13 loads 1 (the number of `write`) into `eax`, and the instruction at +18 is `SYSCALL`. The comparison with `0xfffffffffffff000` tests whether the result lies in the error range; the code at +112 negates it and stores it in `errno`, which lives in thread-local storage addressed through the `fs` register. The first branch handles the common single-threaded case without the cancellation bookkeeping that the multi-threaded path performs.

The same sequence can be written by hand with inline assembly. The program in the following listing performs `write` twice, once with a valid descriptor and once with an invalid one, without calling the C library wrapper.

blocks.title: rawsys.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -o rawsys rawsys.c && ./rawsys
written with a raw SYSCALL instruction
returned 39
write to fd 99 returned -9 (negative errno, -EBADF = -9)
$ strace -e trace=write ./rawsys 2>&1 | grep 'write(99'
write(99, "wri", 3)                     = -1 EBADF (Bad file descriptor)
blocks.title: Raw system calls and the negative-errno convention

blocks.text:
The kernel returned -9 in `rax`. `strace` decodes that value as `-1 EBADF` because it knows the convention, while the raw wrapper exposes the unprocessed value.

#### The cost of the transition and the vDSO

Entering and leaving the kernel is more expensive than an ordinary call because the processor changes privilege, the kernel switches stacks, and on many processors additional mitigations for speculative-execution vulnerabilities add work. The following program measures the cost of four operations: a normal function call, the cheapest system call (`getppid`), the clock read through the C library, and the same clock read forced through the `SYSCALL` instruction.

blocks.title: sysc.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -O1 -o sysc sysc.c && ./sysc
function call        :     1.0 ns/call
getppid() syscall    :   125.2 ns/call
clock_gettime (vDSO) :    26.3 ns/call
clock_gettime (trap) :   154.7 ns/call
$ strace -c -e trace=clock_gettime ./sysc 2>&1 | tail -6 | head -5
clock_gettime (trap) : 13214.6 ns/call
% time     seconds  usecs/call     calls    errors syscall
------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------- ----------------
100.00    3.924013           1   2000000           clock_gettime
------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------- ----------------
blocks.title: Measured on the build machine (typical output of three runs, first run shown)

blocks.text:
A real transition costs roughly 100 to 150 ns, about a hundred times a function call. The line labelled `(vDSO)` is faster because the kernel maps a small code page, the **virtual dynamic shared object** (vDSO), into every process. The C library calls the clock function in that page, which reads a time value that the kernel keeps updated in a shared data page; no ring change occurs. The mapping is visible in `/proc/PID/maps` as `[vdso]` and `[vvar]`. Only a few calls are served this way: `clock_gettime`, `gettimeofday`, `time` and `getcpu`. The last block of the experiment shows the consequence for observation: under `strace`, only the forced-trap calls appear (2,000,000 of them), because the vDSO calls never enter the kernel and therefore cannot be traced. It also shows the cost of tracing, which is the subject of one of the incidents of this chapter.

**Cost of reading the clock (ns per call, measured, log scale)**

function call **1.0**

clock\_gettime via vDSO **26.3**

getppid() trap **117**

clock\_gettime via SYSCALL **150**

same trap, under strace **13215**

vDSO: kernel-supplied code page, SYSCALL path: ring switch, entry code, strace: two ptrace stops per call; no ring change, reads a vvar page dispatch, return the tracer is scheduled twice

*Figure 1.14. A time read through the vDSO costs about 26 ns, a real system call about 150 ns, and the same call under* `strace` *about* *13,000 ns.*

The clock source matters for this mechanism: on this machine `/sys/devices/system/clocksource/clocksource0/current_clocksource` reports `tsc`, which the vDSO can read without entering the kernel. Some virtualised environments use a clock source that the vDSO cannot read, in which case every call to `System.nanoTime` becomes a real system call.

#### How a JVM uses system calls

The JVM itself is a heavy user of three groups. Memory management uses `mmap`, `munmap` and `mprotect` to reserve the heap, to commit pages and to implement safepoint polling and code-cache protection. Thread synchronisation uses `futex` for monitors, `LockSupport.park`, `Thread.sleep` and condition waits. Input and output use `read`, `write`, `openat`, `epoll_wait` and the socket calls. `System.nanoTime` uses `clock_gettime` through the vDSO. The blocked state of a thread can be read without any tracer: the file `/proc/PID/task/TID/syscall` shows the call that a sleeping thread is in.

blocks.code:
$ cat /proc/9254/task/9254/syscall /proc/9254/task/9254/wchan; echo
202 0x7f4c9001b378 0x89 0x0 0x7f4c951fe740 0x0 0xffffffff 0x7f4c951fe610 0x7f4c96898e51
futex_do_wait
blocks.title: The system call in which two JVM threads are blocked (typical output)

blocks.text:
The first number, 202, is `futex`; the second column is the first argument (the address of the lock word) and the third is the operation (`0x89` is `FUTEX_WAIT_BITSET` with the private flag). The thread is the Java `main` thread of `Sleeper`, which is inside `Thread.sleep`, implemented in the JVM as a timed park on a futex.

### Worked trace

#### A C program from `execve` to `exit_group`

The following trace is the output of `strace` for the program `hello` (a single `printf`), reduced to the lines that matter and grouped by phase. The complete trace has 34 calls.

blocks.title: hello.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -O0 -o hello hello.c && strace -o hello.trace ./hello && cat hello.trace
execve("./hello", ["./hello"], 0x7ffe1a132b20 /* 212 vars */) = 0
brk(NULL)                               = 0x5570aacc7000
mmap(NULL, 8192, PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0) = 0x7f8673358000
access("/etc/ld.so.preload", R_OK)      = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/ld.so.cache", O_RDONLY|O_CLOEXEC) = 3
mmap(NULL, 54375, PROT_READ, MAP_PRIVATE, 3, 0) = 0x7f867334a000
close(3)                                = 0
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6", O_RDONLY|O_CLOEXEC) = 3
read(3, "\177ELF\2\1\1\3\0\0\0\0\0\0\0\0\3\0>\0\1\0\0\0\220\243\2\0\0\0\0\0"..., 832) = 832
mmap(0x7f8673028000, 1609728, PROT_READ|PROT_EXEC, ...) = 0x7f8673028000
close(3)                                = 0
arch_prctl(ARCH_SET_FS, 0x7f8673347740) = 0
set_tid_address(0x7f8673347a10)         = 640
mprotect(0x7f8673200000, 16384, PROT_READ) = 0
munmap(0x7f867334a000, 54375)           = 0
fstat(1, {st_mode=S_IFREG|0644, st_size=19, ...}) = 0
getrandom("\xdc\xd8\x7b\x9a\x4b\x2a\x58\x75", 8, GRND_NONBLOCK) = 8
brk(NULL)                               = 0x5570aacc7000
brk(0x5570aace8000)                     = 0x5570aace8000
write(1, "Hello, kernel\n", 14)         = 14
exit_group(0)                           = ?
+++ exited with 0 +++
blocks.title: strace of the dynamically linked hello (typical addresses; trimmed)

blocks.text:
1. `execve` replaces the shell's child with the new program. Everything before the first line of `main` is the work of the dynamic loader and the C library.
2. `brk` **and** `mmap` set up the loader's own memory. The `access("/etc/ld.so.preload")` call fails with `ENOENT`, which is normal: it checks for an optional preload list.
3. `openat("/etc/ld.so.cache")`**,** `mmap`**,** `close` read the cache of library locations, then `openat("libc.so.6")`, `read` of the ELF header and several `mmap` calls map the C library into the address space with the permissions of each segment (read-execute for code, read-only for constants, read-write for data).
4. `arch_prctl(ARCH_SET_FS)` points the `fs` register at the thread control block, which is where `errno` lives. `set_tid_address` registers the address that the kernel clears when the thread exits; the returned value, 640, is the thread identifier.
5. `mprotect` makes the relocated data read-only. `munmap` discards the library cache mapping. `getrandom` seeds the allocator.
6. `fstat(1)` examines standard output. In this run the output was captured to a file (`S_IFREG`), so the C library selects full buffering; on a terminal it selects line buffering and the write would follow the newline immediately. The two `brk` calls grow the heap for the buffer.
7. `write(1, "Hello, kernel\n", 14)` is the single call that the program asked for. It happens at exit, when the buffer is flushed.
8. `exit_group(0)` terminates every thread of the process and returns the status to the parent.

Thirty-three of the 34 calls are overhead of the runtime and one is the work. Linking statically removes the loader's part: the static build of the same program issues 16 calls. The JVM, with a far larger runtime, issues 1,457 for the same single line of output.

**System calls executed to print one line (strace -c)**

C, dynamic libc **34**

C, static libc **16**

Java Hello (JDK 21) **1457**

**Inside the 1457 calls of the JVM run**

futex **285**

mprotect **245**

mmap **238**

rt\_sigprocmask **116**

openat **78**

read **59**

close **58**

*Figure 1.15. The fixed cost of starting a runtime is measured in system calls; the JVM's total is dominated by* `futex` *(thread* *coordination) and by memory-mapping calls, not by file I/O.*

### Hands-on

#### The `strace` toolbox

`strace` runs a program under the kernel's `ptrace` facility and prints every system call with its arguments and its result. The options below cover almost all diagnostic use.

rows: Always for a JVM, which is multi-threaded
Write the trace to a file
Keep the trace apart from the program's output
Attach to a running process (add `-f` for all threads)
Diagnose a stuck service without restarting it
Print a table of counts and times instead of the trace
Sort the `-c` table by call count
Trace only the named calls or a group such as `%file`, `%network`, `%memory`
Show the time spent inside each call
Print a wall-clock time stamp with microseconds
Print the file path next to a file descriptor
Print up to N bytes of string arguments
See more of a read or write
Stop only on the traced calls
blocks.caption: The strace options used in this book.

blocks.text:
#### Follow errors and timing: the open-and-read program

The next program tries to open a file that does not exist, then reads a file that does.

blocks.title: open_fail.c

blocks.code:
$ strace -tt -T -e trace=openat,read,close ./open_fail 2>&1 | grep -v -e ld.so -e libc | tail -7
02:17:05.178913 openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/does-not-exist.conf", O_RDONLY) = -1 ENOENT (...) <0.000011>
02:17:05.180434 openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/hostname", O_RDONLY) = 3 <0.000011>
02:17:05.180518 read(3, "vm\n", 64)     = 3 <0.000012>
02:17:05.180551 close(3)                = 0 <0.000004>
open failed: errno=2 (No such file or directory)
read 3 bytes
02:17:05.180657 +++ exited with 0 +++
$ strace -e trace=%file ./open_fail 2>&1 | tail -5
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6", O_RDONLY|O_CLOEXEC) = 3
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/does-not-exist.conf", O_RDONLY) = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/hostname", O_RDONLY) = 3
open failed: errno=2 (No such file or directory)
read 3 bytes
blocks.title: Timing (-T), time stamps (-tt) and the file group (typical output)

blocks.text:
The pattern that this shows is the most common use of `strace` in operations: the failing call (`ENOENT`) names the path that the program expected, which turns "the application cannot find its configuration" into a precise file name. The `-T` value is the duration of the call; a `read` or `connect` with a large value identifies the slow dependency.

#### Trace and count a JVM

blocks.code:
$ strace -f -c -o java.sc java Hello > /dev/null
$ head -10 java.sc
% time     seconds  usecs/call     calls    errors syscall
------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------- ------------------
 94.71    0.120780         423       285        43 futex
  0.73    0.000934           3       245           mprotect
  0.94    0.001193           5       238           mmap
  0.35    0.000440           3       116           rt_sigprocmask
  0.42    0.000538           6        78        21 openat
  0.24    0.000308           5        59           read
  0.31    0.000397           6        58           close
  0.19    0.000239           4        58           fstat
$ tail -1 java.sc
100.00    0.127520          87      1457        96 total
$ strace -f -o java.full java Hello > /dev/null
$ grep -c clone3 java.full; awk '{print $1}' java.full | sort -u | wc -l
29
18
blocks.title: Counting the system calls of a Java Hello World (typical output; counts vary by about 5 percent)

blocks.text:
The `% time` column is misleading here: 95 percent of the time attributed to `futex` is threads waiting for each other, which is idle time, not work. The reliable columns are `calls` and `errors`. Of the 96 failed calls, most are probes for optional files (`ENOENT`), for example the JVM searching for architecture-specific library variants under `glibc-hwcaps` directories, which is harmless. The trace of 1,821 lines contains 18 distinct thread identifiers and 17 `clone3` calls (the count of 29 above includes lines that `strace` split with `<unfinished ...>` and `resumed`).

The files that the JVM opens are informative too. It reads the module image `lib/modules` (140 MB) and the class data sharing archive `lib/server/classes.jsa`, probes `/proc/self/coredump_filter` and `/etc/passwd`, and reads the control-group files `/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.cfs_quota_us` and `/sys/fs/cgroup/memory/.../memory.limit_in_bytes`. The last group is how the JVM discovers container limits; the chapter on the Linux file-based view explains the consequences.

### Real-world incidents

#### Incident: a Java service burns a core on system time because it writes byte by byte

**Scenario.** An export service writes a CSV file to local disk through a `FileOutputStream` obtained from a legacy helper. The helper writes each character with `write(int)`. The service handles small exports in production without issue, and a new customer requests exports of several million rows.

**Symptoms.** Export requests take minutes. `top` shows the Java process at 100 percent of one core, and the split of CPU time shows a large share of system time (`sy`) alongside user time. Garbage collection logs are quiet and the disk shows little throughput.

**Diagnosis.** The combination of high system time and low disk throughput suggests many small calls into the kernel. `strace -c` counts them.

blocks.title: ByteWriter.java

blocks.code:
$ java ByteWriter unbuffered
unbuffered: 200000 bytes in 165 ms
$ java ByteWriter buffered
buffered: 200000 bytes in 19 ms
$ strace -f -c -o sc_unbuffered.txt java ByteWriter unbuffered > /dev/null
$ head -6 sc_unbuffered.txt | cut -c1-70
% time     seconds  usecs/call     calls    errors syscall
------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------- ------------------
 95.95    4.493343        5673       792        87 futex
  3.92    0.183625           0    200017           write
  0.06    0.002591        1295         2           sched_yield
  0.01    0.000701           7        89        24 openat
$ strace -f -c -o sc_buffered.txt java ByteWriter buffered > /dev/null
$ grep -w write sc_buffered.txt
  0.13    0.000239           5        42           write
blocks.title: Reproduction with 200,000 single-byte writes (typical output)

blocks.text: The unbuffered variant issued 200,017 `write` calls, one per byte, while the buffered variant issued 42 in total. The 200,017 count equals the number of bytes plus 17 calls from the runtime itself, which is a precise signature of a one-call-per-byte loop. The run times (165 ms against 19 ms here) grow linearly with the data, and on a loaded server, where each call also competes with other threads, the system time dominates.

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The helper used an unbuffered stream. Each `write(int)` is a native method that performs one `write` system call, so the cost of the ring transition (about 100 ns plus the file-system work of every call) was paid per byte.

**Fix.** Wrap the stream in `BufferedOutputStream` (8 KiB is the default) or use `Files.newBufferedWriter`; write arrays or strings, not single bytes. For large sequential output, a buffer of 64 KiB or more reduces calls further. The immediate mitigation, before a code change, is to limit export size or to move exports to a queue.

**Prevention.** Search for raw `FileOutputStream` and `FileWriter` use in loops during review. In load tests, record the system call rate: `strace -c -f -p PID` for ten seconds on a staging copy, or `vmstat 1` (column `sy` and `cs`) in production. A rate in the hundreds of thousands per second for one process is a defect, whatever the throughput.

#### Incident: attaching strace to a production JVM makes the outage worse

**Scenario.** A payment service shows intermittent timeouts. An engineer attaches `strace -f -p PID` to the production JVM to find the slow call, with no filter, and sends the output to the terminal.

**Symptoms.** Within seconds the service throughput collapses to a fraction of normal, health checks fail and the orchestrator restarts the instance, which removes the evidence.

**Diagnosis.** The slowdown is caused by the tool. `strace` uses `ptrace` to stop the traced process at the entry and the exit of every system call, wakes the tracer, which decodes and prints the call, and then resumes the process. Every call therefore costs two extra context switches and the work of the tracer. The overhead was measured on the build machine using the byte-writing program above, which performs 200,000 calls.

blocks.code:
$ java ByteWriter unbuffered
unbuffered: 200000 bytes in 73 ms
$ strace -f -e trace=none -o /dev/null java ByteWriter unbuffered
unbuffered: 200000 bytes in 6553 ms
$ strace -f -c -o /dev/null java ByteWriter unbuffered
unbuffered: 200000 bytes in 4770 ms
$ strace -f --seccomp-bpf -e trace=openat -o /dev/null java ByteWriter unbuffered
unbuffered: 200000 bytes in 80 ms
blocks.title: Overhead of different strace modes on the same program (typical output)

blocks.text:
Tracing nothing at all (`-e trace=none`) still slowed the program by a factor of about 90, because the ptrace stops occur for every call regardless of the filter. Counting (`-c`) is cheaper but remains in the same order. The `--seccomp-bpf` option installs a filter in the kernel so that only the selected calls stop the process; with a filter on a rarely used call, the run time was almost unchanged (80 ms against 73 ms). **Traced thread Kernel strace (tracer)**

**default mode: every system call**

write(1, buf, 1)

stop at entry, wake tracer

tracer decodes and prints the call

PTRACE\_SYSCALL: resume

kernel runs write

stop at exit, wake tracer

resume

return to thread

**--seccomp-bpf -e trace=openat: a call outside the filter**

write(1, buf, 1)

filter says no stop: return

*Figure 1.17. Without the filter option,* `strace` *stops the traced thread twice per system call and the tracer is scheduled twice; with* `--seccomp-bpf` *the kernel stops the thread only for the selected calls.*

**Root cause.** An unfiltered ptrace attach on a process that executes tens of thousands of system calls per second. The JVM of a busy service performs most of them in `futex`, `read`, `write` and `epoll_wait`.

**Fix.** Mitigation: detach (`Ctrl-C` ends `strace` and the process continues), and re-run on one instance removed from the load balancer. Correct procedure: use `strace -c -p PID` for a few seconds to see which calls dominate; then use a filter with `--seccomp-bpf`, for example `-f --seccomp-bpf -e trace=connect,sendto,recvfrom -T -tt -o` `/tmp/t.txt`; or use the JVM's own tools (`jcmd PID Thread.print`, Java Flight Recorder), which do not stop every call.

**Prevention.** Document the safe procedure in the runbook. Prefer sampling tools in production. Perf-based tracing (`perf trace`) and eBPF tools have lower overhead; they are not available on the build machine of this book and were not run. Never write a trace to the terminal of a busy process, and write the file to a local disk with sufficient free space.

### Questions to expect

#### Questions and model answers

1. **What is a system call and why is it needed?** The interface by which a user program requests a privileged operation from the kernel. It is needed because user code runs in ring 3 and cannot touch devices, page tables or other processes' memory.
2. **Describe what happens between** `write()` **in C and the data reaching the device.** The wrapper loads `rax` with the call number and the argument registers, executes `SYSCALL`; the processor enters ring 0 at the kernel entry point; the kernel dispatches through the table to `write`, validates the descriptor, copies data to the file or device layer; the result goes into `rax` and `SYSRET` returns.
3. **How is an error reported by a system call?** The kernel returns a negative error number in `rax`; the C wrapper stores the positive value in `errno` and returns -1.
4. **Why is a system call more expensive than a function call?** It changes privilege level, switches stacks, runs the entry and exit code, and on some processors includes mitigations for speculative-execution attacks. The measured cost here is 100 to 150 ns against 1 ns.
5. **What is the vDSO and which calls use it?** A kernel-provided page mapped into every process that implements some calls, such as `clock_gettime`, entirely in user space by reading kernel-updated data. It avoids the ring transition.
6. **What does** `strace -c` **show and what is the caveat in the** `% time` **column?** The count, error count and time of each call. The time includes waiting, so blocking calls such as `futex` and `epoll_wait` dominate without indicating work.
7. **Why does** `strace` **slow the traced process so much?** It stops the process at each call's entry and exit through `ptrace`, and the tracer must run, decode and resume it. `--seccomp-bpf` limits the stops to selected calls.
8. **How would you find which file an application fails to open?** `strace -f -e trace=%file -o out.txt` `command`, then search for `ENOENT` or `EACCES` in the trace; the argument of the failing `openat` is the path.
9. **A Java program calls** `System.out.print` **for each of a million characters and is slow. Why?** `System.out` is a `PrintStream`, which flushes to a `FileOutputStream`; with autoflush or without buffering, each call can become a system call. Building one string or using a buffered writer reduces the number of calls.
10. **How can a blocked thread's system call be found without tracing?** `cat /proc/PID/task/TID/syscall` shows the call number and arguments; `/proc/PID/task/TID/wchan` shows the kernel function where the thread sleeps.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
The system call is the single, narrow gate between a process and the kernel, and observing it explains most process behaviour.

- Convention: number in `rax`, arguments in `rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8, r9`, `SYSCALL` to enter, result in `rax` with negative values meaning `-errno`.
- A transition costs roughly 100 to 150 ns on the build machine; the vDSO serves clock reads without a transition (about 26 ns).
- A Java Hello World performs about 1,450 system calls (futex, mprotect, mmap dominate) against 34 for the equivalent C program.
- `strace -f -c` counts calls, `-e trace=%file` finds missing files, `-T` finds slow calls, `/proc/PID/task/TID/syscall` shows a blocked call without tracing.
- `strace` slows a process by about two orders of magnitude; use `--seccomp-bpf` with a filter, or sampling tools, on production systems.

When a machine is powered on, nothing is running: memory is uninitialised, the kernel is a file on a disk, and no process exists. The boot sequence is the chain of small programs that each prepare the machine for the next one, ending in the first user-space process, which starts everything else. Understanding the chain turns vague symptoms (the server does not come back after a reboot, the service starts by hand but not at boot, the container stops after one signal) into questions with specific places to look. This chapter follows the sequence from firmware to the service manager and then concentrates on `systemd`, which starts almost every service on a modern Linux server.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The boot sequence

1. **Firmware.** The processor starts at a fixed address in firmware, either the legacy BIOS or UEFI. The firmware tests and initialises the hardware, then looks for a bootable device. UEFI reads files from a FAT-formatted EFI System Partition and can verify signatures (Secure Boot); legacy BIOS reads the first 512-byte sector of the disk.
2. **Bootloader.** A program such as GRUB loads the kernel image and an initial RAM file system (initramfs) into memory, passes the **kernel command line**, and jumps to the kernel. On virtual machines that use a direct-boot mechanism, the hypervisor performs this step and no bootloader exists.
3. **Kernel start-up.** The kernel decompresses itself, sets up memory management and the interrupt tables, starts the scheduler and initialises the built-in drivers. It then mounts the initial RAM file system as the temporary root.
4. **Initramfs.** A small archive that contains the drivers and tools needed to reach the real root file system: disk controller and file-system modules, RAID or LVM assembly, decryption of an encrypted volume. It finds and mounts the real root and switches to it.
5. **PID 1.** The kernel executes the first user-space program, `/sbin/init`, which is `systemd` on current mainstream distributions. It receives process identifier 1 and has no parent to report to; it is the ancestor of every other process.
6. **User space start-up.** The init system mounts the remaining file systems, starts services in dependency order, and reaches the default target (for a server, `multi-user.target`).

blocks.text:
#### The kernel command line

The bootloader passes text parameters that configure the kernel and the init process. They are visible in `/proc/cmdline`. The build machine of this book is a micro virtual machine that starts the kernel directly, and its command line shows the typical elements:

blocks.code:
$ cat /proc/cmdline | fold -w 90
mitigations=auto,no_guest_host,no_guest_guest deferred_init=lazy dhash_entries=131072 ihash_entr
ies=65536 console=ttyS0 reboot=k panic=1 nomodule random.trust_cpu=1 ipv6.disable=1 swiotlb=nof
orce psi=1 rdinit=/process_api -- --firecracker-init --addr 0.0.0.0:2024 --max-ws-buffer-size 32
768 --block-local-connections --listen-vsock-port 2024 --log-vsock-port 5002
$ ls /sys/firmware; ls /sys/firmware/efi
acpi  memmap
ls: cannot access '/sys/firmware/efi': No such file or directory
blocks.title: The kernel command line of the build machine

blocks.text:
The parameters that matter to an engineer:

- `console=ttyS0` sends kernel messages to a serial port, the usual console of a virtual machine.
- `panic=1` reboots one second after a kernel panic; `reboot=k` selects the reboot method.
- `nomodule` forbids loading kernel modules; that is why `/proc/modules` does not exist on this machine.
- `ipv6.disable=1` and `psi=1` toggle the IPv6 stack and enable pressure stall information, which provides `/proc/pressure/*` used in the diagnostic chapters.
- `mitigations=auto` selects the default speculative-execution mitigations, which affect the cost of system calls.
- `rdinit=/process_api` names the program to run as PID 1 from the initial RAM file system, instead of `/sbin/init`; everything after the `--` is passed to that program as arguments. On the build machine the first process is therefore the control agent of the sandbox, which agrees with the `ps -p 1` result of the first chapter. The absence of `/sys/firmware/efi` confirms that no UEFI firmware was involved.

On a server the same file contains `root=UUID=...`, `ro` and often `quiet` and cgroup options such as `systemd.unified_cgroup_hierarchy=1`. A parameter that is wrong after a change to the bootloader configuration is a common cause of a machine that does not return after a reboot.

#### PID 1 and the init system

PID 1 has two roles that no other process has. It **starts** the system, and it **adopts orphans**: when a process exits while its children are alive, the kernel re-parents the children to PID 1, and PID 1 must call `wait` to collect their exit status or they become zombies. In addition, the kernel treats PID 1 specially for signals: a signal for which PID 1 has installed no handler is ignored, not applied with the default action, so that a mistaken `kill` cannot take the system down. The same rules apply to the first process of a PID namespace, which is what the entry point of a container is. The experiment below creates such a namespace with `unshare` and demonstrates the signal rule.

blocks.code:
$ unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc --kill-child bash -c \
    'echo "inside: pid=$$"; ps -o pid,ppid,comm; kill -TERM $$; echo "survived SIGTERM"'
inside: pid=1
    PID    PPID COMMAND
      1       0 bash
      2       1 ps
survived SIGTERM
blocks.title: The first process of a new PID namespace ignores an unhandled SIGTERM

blocks.text:
Inside the namespace the shell has PID 1 and its parent is 0 (outside the namespace). The `kill -TERM $$` is sent to PID 1 itself and has no effect because bash has no handler for it in this context. The consequence for containers is direct: a Java application started as `CMD java -jar app.jar` in a container becomes PID 1; the JVM installs a handler for `SIGTERM`, so it does shut down, but a shell script wrapper that starts the JVM without `exec` does not forward the signal, and an orphaned grandchild is never reaped. The container chapter returns to this.

#### systemd units, targets and dependencies

`systemd` models the system as a graph of **units**. A unit is described by a text file in `/lib/systemd/system` (packaged units), `/etc/systemd/system` (administrator units and overrides) or `/run/systemd/system`. The common unit types are in the following table.

rows: A process or group of processes that systemd starts and supervises
A named synchronisation point that groups units
A listening socket that starts a service on the first connection
A schedule that activates another unit
A mount point, usually generated from `/etc/fstab`
Activates a unit when a path changes
blocks.caption: Common systemd unit types.

blocks.text:
Ordering and requirement are separate concepts, and confusing them is the most frequent cause of start-up problems.

- **Requirement**: `Wants=` (soft: start the other unit, tolerate its failure) and `Requires=` (hard: if the other unit fails to start or stops, this one stops).
- **Ordering**: `After=` and `Before=` say in which order two units start. They say nothing about whether the other unit is started at all.

A unit that declares `After=postgresql.service` without `Wants=` or `Requires=` is started after PostgreSQL only if something else started PostgreSQL. Conversely, `Requires=postgresql.service` without `After=` starts both at the same time.

**Ordering (After=): arrows point to the unit that starts later**

local-fs.target sysinit.target basic.target **multi-user.target** graphical.target

*default target of a server*

WantedBy=multi-user.target

Wants + After After network.target network-online.target **orders.service** postgresql.service

start-order (After=) pulled in by an \[Install\] WantedBy=

*Figure 1.19. Targets form the skeleton of the boot: a service attaches itself to a target through* `WantedBy=` *in its* `[Install]` *section,* *and the default target pulls in everything below it.* The **start of a service** proceeds as follows. The manager resolves the dependencies of the unit and queues start jobs for them. For a unit of `Type=simple`, which is the default and the usual choice for a Spring Boot executable jar, `systemd` creates a control group for the service, applies the settings of the unit (user, working directory, resource limits such as `LimitNOFILE`), forks, executes the command, and considers the unit started as soon as the process has been forked. For `Type=notify` the unit is started only when the program reports readiness through the notification socket; `Type=forking` is for traditional daemons that fork into the background and exit. Standard output and error of the service are connected to the journal.

blocks.alt: systemd (PID 1) Kernel Service process journald | mkdir system.slice/orders.service (cgroup) | fork() > child pid 1894 | child starts in the new cgroup | chdir, setuid(orders), LimitNOFILE | stdout and stderr > journal socket | execve(/usr/bin/java ...) | Type=simple: unit is active | log lines (Started OrdersApplication) | SIGCHLD + exit status on death

blocks.text:
`execve`*, and log the output; the journal receives everything the process writes to its standard streams.*

Three commands give the state of the system: `systemctl status UNIT` shows the state, the main process and the most recent log lines; `journalctl -u UNIT -b` shows the logs of one unit since boot; `systemctl list-dependencies` `UNIT` shows the dependency tree. The state of a service follows the finite state machine shown below.

start forked stop inactive activating active deactivating (dead) (start) (running) (stop)

exited after SIGTERM, status 0 or SuccessExitStatus

non-zero exit, signal, timeout

Restart=no (default): Restart= applies, start limit hit **failed** stays failed, nobody notices after RestartSec stays failed

**Restart policy decides between the green path and a permanent failed state**

*Figure 1.21. A service that exits with a failure moves to* `failed`*, and the* `Restart=` *setting determines whether it is started again;* *after too many restarts within* `StartLimitIntervalSec`*, systemd gives up and stays in* `failed`*.*

### Worked trace

#### Typical timeline of a server boot

The numbers below are the typical output of `systemd-analyze` on a cloud virtual machine of the kind that runs Java services; they illustrate the proportions and were not measured on the build machine, which does not run systemd. The same command on a real server prints the stage times in its first line.

$ systemd-analyze blame | head -5
